The sonographic features deteriorated slightly to that observed on D1 with the nodal shape becoming more lobulated and some loss of hilarious delineation. Interruption to the capsule was also observed indicating progressive perinodal reaction and oedema.

By D11, the patient was reported to have improved clinically and only mild plague symptoms remained. While the pain score further decreased to 3/10 and no changes to the clinical characteristics of the bubo were observed, further radiological progression was present. The capsule became indistinct and irregular, the hilum was no longer visible and perinodal oedema had progressed further.

By D4, while the bubo remained hard and the pain score decreased to 6/10, oedema was noted on palpation. On ultrasound examination the bubo demonstrated interval enlargement with a rounded shape, reduced hilar definition and blurring of the capsule.
89.Rationale: The passage documents that sonographic morphology (capsule, hilum, shape) can change over time even as clinical findings may not, which shows morphology evolves. However, the question asks about assessing changes in lymph node size over time using physical exam alone. Morphologic variability affects interpretation and may complicate assessment, but the passage identifies measurement error of digital callipers (physical measurement tool) as the primary factor undermining reliability in tracking size. Therefore although morphology changes are documented, they are not presented as the most critical reason physical examination alone fails to reliably track size changes; measurement inaccuracy is.

89.Option: The absence of a standardized clinical definition for 'enlarged lymph node' across health centers introduces inconsistency in physical examination-based size tracking
Evidence: Participants were retrospectively categorised as “plague cases” or “non-cases” according to the WHO plague case definition following receipt of laboratory results from samples collected as part of routine care under the national plague surveillance programme.
Data were collected using a standardised paper Case Report Form (CRF), which was subsequently transcribed into REDCap.
89.Rationale: The passage indicates use of standard procedures (the WHO plague case definition and a standardised CRF) for case classification and data collection, which argues against the option's claim of an absence of standardized definition across centers. The text provides no evidence that a lack of a standardized clinical definition for 'enlarged lymph node' was a problem. Thus this option is not supported by the passage.

89.Option: High measurement error in digital calliper assessments, particularly in the inguinal region where most buboes are located, introduces significant bias in tracking size changes over time
Evidence: Sixteen digital calliper measurements were compared to corresponding ultrasound measurements of the same enlarged lymph nodes. Substantial discrepancies were observed across all anatomical zones when comparing the two methods (Table 2).

Consistent with the findings in a separate study evaluating measurement validity and reliability of artificial buboes [12], the digital calliper measurements recorded in this study differed substantially from those measured by ultrasound, which was used as the reference standard.
Inguinal lymph nodes exhibited greater variability, with a mean absolute difference of 3.15mm (range: 1.14–4.93mm) and a mean percentage difference of 112.8% (range: 44.0%–159.9%).

In addition to the lack of association between bubo morphology and treatment response, this study therefore demonstrates that using a digital calliper to measure buboes in clinical trials may lead to incorrect classifications of patients as either having or (more likely) not having had a treatment response.
89.Rationale: The passage directly documents large and systematic measurement error when using a digital calliper compared to ultrasound, with especially large percentage differences in the inguinal zone where most buboes occurred. The authors explicitly conclude that calliper-based measurements may 'lead to incorrect classifications' of treatment response. Because tracking size changes over time depends on accurate and precise measurements, this documented measurement error most critically undermines the reliability of using physical examination (and simple callipers) alone to assess size changes.

89.Option: The lack of consistent correlation between clinical symptoms and sonographic features of the bubo limits the ability to use physical examination to assess treatment response
Evidence: Our findings highlight the absence of an observed association between bubo size, morphology, and clinical status, which is particularly evident in the case reports.
Both cases presented are confirmed cases of plague.

By D11, the patient was reported to have improved clinically and only mild plague symptoms remained. While the pain score further decreased to 3/10 and no changes to the clinical characteristics of the bubo were observed, further radiological progression was present.

By D11, the patient’s clinical status had improved overall but a few mild persistent symptoms remained. The size of the bubo decreased from D4 to 53.2mm but remained larger, with loss of the normal capsule and no clear hilar echogenicity.
89.Rationale: The passage does show an absence of correlation between clinical status and sonographic features — e.g., clinical improvement occurred while sonographic progression persisted — which undermines the use of bubo size as a surrogate for treatment response. However, the question asks about reliability of using physical examination alone to assess changes in lymph node size over time. That specific reliability problem is most directly and critically driven by measurement error (see Option 3). While the lack of correlation means that even perfectly measured size changes might not reflect clinical improvement, it is a separate problem (validity of size as an outcome) rather than the primary measurement reliability issue. Therefore this option is not the best single answer to the question as phrased.

90.Option: The increasing number of human cases in Hainan Province over time indicates a growing spillover risk due to climate change and urbanization
Evidence: Hainan is located in the tropical region of China, which is favorable for the reproduction of small mammals.
According to the China Public Health Science Data Center, the number of HFRS cases in Hainan Province exhibited an increasing trend from 2014 to 2019 (https://www.phsciencedata.cn/Share).

With global climate change and the deepening of China’s exchanges with the international community in transportation, trade, and tourism, pathogen-carrying organisms and the pathogens they carry can be introduced between international ports via vehicles, containers, goods, mail, etc., increasing the risk of imported diseases and potentially triggering domestic transmission [12].
90.Rationale: The passage documents both (a) increases in HFRS cases in Hainan (2014–2019) and (b) concerns about climate change and increased movement of pathogen-carrying organisms via trade and travel. However, the linkage in the passage is circumstantial: while rising cases are noted and broad mechanisms (climate change, increased transport) are described as increasing risk, the text does not provide direct evidence that the observed increase in Hainan is caused specifically by climate change or urbanization. Therefore this option overstates the causal inference and is not the strongest single factor supported by the study.

90.Option: The presence of multiple hantavirus subtypes in overlapping regions increases the likelihood of spillover due to viral recombination and host adaptation
Evidence: given the high diversity of HVs subtypes and the complexity of viral strains carried by hosts (e.g., rodents), methods in this study poses certain challenges for the simultaneous differentiation and identification of multiple HVs subtypes—particularly in the overlapping regions of the Indian Ocean periphery and Southeast Asia, where viral strain coexistence is highly prevalent [49].
90.Rationale: The passage does state there is high diversity of HV subtypes and coexistence of strains in overlapping regions, which could theoretically affect viral evolution. However, the paper does not provide direct evidence that recombination or host-adaptive events driven by subtype coexistence are driving spillover risk. The text frames subtype diversity primarily as a challenge for detection and identification, not as demonstrated mechanistic evidence of increased spillover. Thus this option is not strongly supported by the study’s findings.

90.Option: The use of RT-PCR in detection methods leads to underestimation of true prevalence, thereby increasing the perceived risk of spillover in Southeast Asia
Evidence: Both IFA and ELISA detection methods showed higher prevalence than RT-PCR, which is consistent with Obando-Rico et al. [47].

The reason for this result may be that IFA and ELISA detect antigens or antibodies, thereby reflecting prior exposure of the virus and a relative higher prevalence. While RT-PCR detects the current HVs infection in small mammals.

The prevalence for IFA, ELISA, RT-PCR were 9.35% (95%CI, 4.85%-17.26%, p < 0.01), 10.68% (95%CI, 4.05%-25.33%, p < 0.01), and 2.29% (95%CI, 0.87%-5.91%, p < 0.01), respectively, with ELISA showing the highest rate.
90.Rationale: The passage shows RT-PCR yields lower prevalence estimates than serologic methods because it detects current infection while serology reflects past exposure. That implies RT-PCR can underestimate cumulative exposure. However, the option claims this underestimation "thereby increases the perceived risk of spillover," which is logically inconsistent: underestimation would tend to understate risk, not increase perceived risk. Also, while detection method differences affect measurement, they do not in themselves demonstrate a higher ecological risk of spillover. Therefore this option is not supported as stated.

90.Option: High population densities of small mammals driven by warm, humid climates and human-modified environments increase the likelihood of hantavirus spillover in Southeast Asia
Evidence: The transmission of HVs is primarily related to the population of small animal hosts.
Southeast Asia is recognized as the origin of rodents, with more that 35 species of rodents in this region [26].

The temperature and humidity is high in this region, it could create favorable conditions for the survival and reproduction of small mammals. It leads to an increase in the population of small mammals, thereby the high prevalence of HVs [43].
The warm and humid climate of low-latitude regions facilitates small mammal reproduction, leading to higher population densities and enhanced survival of HVs [43].

Indonesia has large areas of farmland and a suitable climate, while Singapore is densely populated and generates substantial waste [39]. Both of these factors provide ideal habitats for small mammals and contribute to a higher prevalence of HVs.
90.Rationale: The passage repeatedly links higher small-mammal population densities—driven by warm, humid climates and human-altered habitats (farmland, dense urban waste environments)—to higher HV prevalence. It also explicitly states that transmission is primarily related to host population size. These ecological and geographic factors provide a clear, directly supported mechanism by which spillover risk to humans would be amplified for a rodent-borne virus maintained in asymptomatic reservoirs, making this the factor most strongly supported by the study.

90.Option: The high prevalence of hantavirus in bats in Southeast Asia indicates a major reservoir role, increasing spillover risk through direct human contact
Evidence: The prevalence of HVs in rodents, shrews, bats were 8.41% (95%CI, 5.35%-12.99%, p < 0.05), 3.90% (95%CI, 1.09%-13.05%, p < 0.05), 1.64% (95%CI, 0.41%-3.16%, p > 0.05), respectively.
Notably, the HVs data of bats should not be directly pooled with that of rodents or shrews for comparative analysis, given the substantial disparities in research contexts.

Unlike the aforementioned small mammals, for which both molecular (RT-PCR) and serological (IFA/ELISA) data are available, current prevalence of HVs in bats is limited to genome detection by RT-PCR alone, and lacked to serological validation (e.g., antibody detection). The number of studies focusing on bats is significantly smaller than that on rodents, resulting in insufficient research coverage and limited data support.

Therefore, the absence of statistical significance in the prevalence of HVs in bats observed in this study more likely underestimated the limitations of current research rather than reflects a true absence of epidemiological risk.
90.Rationale: The passage reports a low and not statistically significant pooled prevalence for bats (1.64%) and emphasizes that bat data are limited, based only on RT-PCR with scarce serological confirmation and few studies. It explicitly cautions against pooling bat data with rodent data and notes insufficient evidence to conclude a major reservoir role. Thus the assertion that bats have high prevalence and are a primary driver of spillover in Southeast Asia is not supported by the study’s findings.

91.Option: A temporary decline in reported cases during 2020 likely reflects surveillance disruption rather than a true reduction in disease burden
Evidence: There was a substantial decrease in the number of reported cases and deaths due to CE and AE in 2020 (Fig 1 and Tables 1 and 2).

This was in the same year as the start of the COVID 19 pandemic and hence this decrease in reported incidence of echinococcosis may be due to the health services having to manage the large numbers of COVID 19 patients and thus fewer resources were availbale to investigate and treat cases of suspected echinococcosis.
91.Rationale: The passage explicitly notes a marked drop in reported cases and deaths in 2020 and directly cautions that this likely reflects disruption of health services during the COVID-19 pandemic (fewer resources for investigation and treatment), not necessarily a true reduction in underlying disease burden. Such surveillance disruption is a pattern that would not be captured by annual incidence rates alone if those rates rely on notifications.

91.Option: The increasing treatment costs in 2020, despite a decline in reported cases, suggest that the disease is becoming more severe or resistant to therapy, indicating a change in pathogenicity
Evidence: The sharp rise in treatment costs—particularly by 1.4 times noted in the year 2020 compared to 2017—reflects both increased awareness and reporting of the disease as well as potentially rising prices for medical care and pharmaceuticals.
Treatment costs are highly variable depending on the local costs of medical treatment.
91.Rationale: While the passage documents rising treatment costs in 2020, the authors attribute the rise to increased awareness/reporting and rising medical care and pharmaceutical prices, not to increased severity or therapeutic resistance. There is no direct evidence presented that the pathogens have become more virulent or resistant; therefore inferring a change in pathogenicity is unsupported by the provided data.

91.Option: The higher case fatality rate for AE compared to CE, particularly among children, indicates a shift toward more aggressive disease manifestation in younger populations
Evidence: An analysis of the reported cases of a 6-year period as a whole showed that for the period 2015–2020 the case fatality rate for AE was 3.6 times higher than for CE.
For AE 36 cases from 1,223 registered cases had a fatal outcome (2.9%) whilst for CE there were where 55 fatalities from 6,576 registered cases (0.9%) (p < 0.0001).

For children under 14 years of age there were three fatal cases of AE from 30 registered case (10%), which was not significantly different from the adult case fatality rate of 33 fatal cases from 1,193 registered cases (p = 0.055).
For CE there were no fatal cases reported among the 1,136 registered pediatric cases, compared to 55 deaths from the 4,940 registered cases in adults (p < 0.0001, Tables 1 and 2).
91.Rationale: The data show AE has a higher case fatality rate than CE and that some pediatric AE deaths occurred. However, the passage notes the pediatric AE fatality rate was not statistically different from adults (p=0.055), and there is no temporal trend presented indicating an increasing burden in children specifically. Thus the evidence does not support asserting a shift toward more aggressive disease in younger populations.

91.Option: An increasing proportion of recurrent cases over time suggests that the disease is becoming more difficult to treat and may indicate a shift toward a more chronic and persistent form of echinococcosis
Evidence: For CE the proportion of cases that were primary cases was 84.7% on average with recurrent cases accounting for the remaining 15.3% of cases. The proportion of recurrent cases for AE was 28.0%.
Of the total number of cases undergoing surgical treatment, the proportion of recurrences in AE was 1.8 times higher than in CE (p < 0.05).
Compared to 2015, there has been an increase in the incidence of recurrent cases rate since 2016, with a peak in 2018 of 4.4 per 100,000 and a subsequent downward trend by 2020 to 1.7 per 100,000.
91.Rationale: The passage documents rising recurrence rates (with a peak in 2018) and substantial proportions of recurrent cases, especially for AE. An increasing share of recurrent cases signals more relapses or chronicity that annual incidence alone (new cases per year) may under-represent, thereby indicating a possible shift toward more persistent disease dynamics or challenges in achieving cure.

91.Option: The increasing prevalence of multiple-organ localization in CE cases suggests a change in transmission dynamics or parasite virulence, indicating a more invasive form of the disease
Evidence: the clinical manifestations of CE are more diverse, and the economic burden of cases with multiple localization more than 23 million KGS, i.e., 270 thousand US$.
This indicates a late detection of this form of clinical manifestation of CE.
91.Rationale: Although the passage notes cases with multiple localization and substantial economic burden, the authors interpret this as indicating late detection rather than a change in transmission dynamics or increased parasite virulence. There is no presented evidence of rising prevalence of multi-organ disease over time or of changing parasite invasiveness, so the option's causal inference is unsupported.

92.Option: The absence of arbovirus detections in 2021 and 2022 samples may reflect a true absence of circulation, as dengue transmission patterns can vary significantly by year and location
Evidence: The lack of DENV in the 617 samples screened from 2021 and 2022 was unexpected and is potentially a result of degraded sample quality from the used RDTs.
These findings confirm that DENV was circulating both within Haiti and throughout Hispaniola between 2021–2022.
92.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that dengue was known to be circulating in Haiti during 2021–2022 and calls the absence of DENV detections in the 617 samples "unexpected," attributing the discrepancy to degraded sample quality rather than a true absence of circulation. Therefore, claiming a true absence of circulation as the most likely contributor conflicts with the passage's evidence and interpretation.

92.Option: Degradation of viral RNA over time due to prolonged room-temperature storage of RDTs likely led to false-negative results in 2021 and 2022 samples
Evidence: The lack of DENV in the 617 samples screened from 2021 and 2022 was unexpected and is potentially a result of degraded sample quality from the used RDTs.

Given that previous studies have demonstrated reduced viral RNA recovery from RDTs stored at room temperature for extended periods of time, along with the observed loss of viral RNA upon extraction from RDTs, there may be instances of missed arbovirus case detections within this study, especially if the patient had a low-level viremia.
The malaria RDTs used in this study were stored at room temperature, and for some samples these storage conditions lasted for more than 2 years.
These data suggest a decrease in sample stability of about 1 log over the three-year collection period.
92.Rationale: The authors repeatedly identify degraded sample quality and reduced viral RNA recovery from RDTs stored at room temperature for extended durations as a likely reason for missed detections in 2021–2022. They note room-temperature storage for >2 years and present RNase P Cq data indicating loss of sample stability. This directly supports that RNA degradation due to prolonged room-temperature storage is the most probable contributor to the absence of detections in those years.

92.Option: The lack of arbovirus detections in 2021 and 2022 samples may be due to insufficient sample size, as only 617 samples were tested from those years
Evidence: The lack of DENV in the 617 samples screened from 2021 and 2022 was unexpected and is potentially a result of degraded sample quality from the used RDTs.

Factors leading to this discrepancy of DENV detection instances may include spatiotemporal variations of DENV transmission patterns that vary by year, or relate to TNA product quality, as discussed below.
92.Rationale: Although the passage mentions 617 samples from 2021–2022, the authors do not attribute the absence of detections primarily to insufficient sample size. Instead they highlight degraded sample/TNA quality and spatiotemporal variation as explanations. The text does not present lack of sample size as the most likely cause, so this option is not supported as the primary factor.

92.Option: The absence of arbovirus detections in 2021 and 2022 samples may be due to the use of a non-specific flavivirus assay that failed to detect DENV-2, the serotype previously circulating in Haiti
Evidence: Samples were tested for flaviviruses using a real-time RT-PCR assay modified from Patel and colleagues targeting a conserved region of the flavivirus nsp5 gene [22].
Sanger sequencing of selected flavivirus-positive samples was conducted to identify the specific flavivirus species.
Sanger sequencing ... identifying DENV as the only flavivirus species present within the samples.
Given this information, all flavivirus positive and indeterminate samples (n = 73) were tested using the DENV quadraplex assay, identifying 68 samples positive for DENV-3.
92.Rationale: The investigators used a conserved flavivirus nsp5 assay as an initial screen, followed by Sanger sequencing and a DENV serotype-specific (quadraplex) RT-PCR to identify serotypes. The passage reports successful identification of DENV-3 where flaviviruses were detected, indicating the assay strategy was capable of detecting and typing DENV. There is no evidence in the text that the assay failed specifically to detect DENV-2; instead, the authors point to degraded RNA and sample stability as reasons for non-detection in 2021–2022.

92.Option: The absence of arbovirus detections in 2021 and 2022 samples may be due to the presence of Plasmodium falciparum, which has been shown to reduce viral loads for arboviruses such as CHIKV
Evidence: Two instances of DENV-3 co-infections with Plasmodium falciparum were detected in this study, bothsamples coming from Les Anglais.
This may have also impacted arbovirus detection in RDT-positive samples, given that Plasmodium infections have been shown to reduce viral loads for arboviruses such as CHIKV [32].
92.Rationale: The passage acknowledges that Plasmodium infections can reduce arboviral loads and that this could impact detection in RDT-positive (malaria-positive) samples. However, only two DENV-3/Plasmodium co-infections were observed, and the authors emphasize degraded sample quality and storage-related RNA loss as the primary explanations for the overall lack of detections in 2021–2022. Thus while Plasmodium co-infection could contribute in individual cases, it is unlikely to be the main factor accounting for the broad absence across the 617 samples.
